source.title: Incorporating Hierarchical Semantics in Sparse Autoencoder Architectures
source.authors: Mark Muchane; Sean M. Richardson; Kiho Park; Victor Veitch

record.tranche_reason: The study measures feature absorption as dictionary width changes using a first-letter classification benchmark, a different measurement from directly matching coarse and fine SAE features.
record.gate_note: Figure 5a and its accompanying description report absorption results relevant to feature splitting. The paper does not report direct measurements of whether child features partition a parent feature's inputs or lie near its direction. Reconstruction results and the cross-language feature-redundancy comparison do not directly test the listed claim versions.
record.test_reason: Figure 5a reports SAEBench first-letter absorption scores on Gemma 2-2B layer 20 for standard TopK SAEs at 8k, 16k and 32k latents, alongside H-SAEs. This is a result on whether absorption persists as width changes (V4). It also bears on whether a change in SAE design reduces absorption (V6). The metric derives from the original absorption work but is applied to self-trained SAEs in a new architecture comparison, so T2.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is partly right but incomplete. The authors conclude that H-SAE dramatically improves reconstruction and moderately improves top-level interpretability. They also report that it reduces absorption and slows its growth with width, reduces cross-language feature redundancy, learns hierarchical semantics (shown qualitatively), and is computationally efficient.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares a hierarchical mixture-of-experts SAE architecture, with a top-level SAE and expert-specific sublatents, against a standard TopK SAE; it does not reproduce the original feature-matching or splitting measurement.
record.method_sensitivity: Architecture (standard SAE versus H-SAE) and dictionary width; H-SAE is also evaluated with 16 or 64 sublatents per expert.

fits_no_version.finding: Fig 5b: across language pairs, the H-SAE's top-8 feature sets for translated tokens differ less than the standard SAE's (e.g. English–French 8.448 vs 9.772).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Standard SAEs learn language-specific duplicate features that the underlying model shares across languages.

fits_no_version.finding: Fig 3: the H-SAE has lower 1−explained variance and lower 1−CE loss score than a standard SAE at each width; the 64-sublatent H-SAE roughly matches a larger standard SAE.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Hierarchical SAE architectures improve reconstruction at fixed top-level width.

record.problems: The absorption result is shown only in a plot, without values or uncertainty reported in the text. The benchmark is an indirect measure of the claimed splitting geometry and does not directly test feature-input coverage or direction similarity.

untested.parts: Not tested: whether finer features replace a coarse feature, cover its inputs, or lie near its direction as width grows. The absorption score does not measure this, despite the caption calling it 'feature splitting'.
Not tested: splitting across open SAE releases, or matching of coarse and fine features at scale. Only self-trained SAEs on Gemma 2-2B are used.
Not tested: whether standard-SAE split features form nested, geometrically close families. H-SAE hierarchy is imposed by design and shown only qualitatively.
Not tested: varying sparsity (k is fixed at 32) and direct parent/child firing analysis.
Not tested: decomposition of larger-SAE latents into smaller ones, or novel latents.
Not tested: whether splitting reflects the model's own units. Matryoshka SAEs are not tested; the change tested is an architecture with an added loss term, not the objective alone.

record.verdict_notes: The Fig 5a caption equates higher absorption with 'greater feature splitting'. The metric measures absorption, hence the V1 unlinking. The trend with width for the standard SAE is inferred from the phrase 'decreases the rate of increase in absorption as width increases'. Exact values are not in the text. No uncertainty is reported, and the study uses a single seed and layer.

versions.untested_parts: The first-letter absorption benchmark is an indirect measure; the study does not test whether fine features jointly cover a coarse feature's inputs or lie near its direction.
No test of the pattern across large models or open SAE releases.
The study does not test whether size-induced split features form geometrically close nested families mirroring a model's concept hierarchy.
The benchmark measures absorption indirectly; the study does not directly test parent-child firing at takeover points or vary sparsity to see whether that behavior changes.
No decomposition of larger-SAE latents into smaller-SAE latents or test for novel latents.
The study does not establish that the standard SAE objective produces splitting on correlated or hierarchical inputs, or test Matryoshka SAEs.

source_check.notes: All absorption values are figure-only (Fig 5a); the text says only that H-SAE lowers absorption and slows its rise with width. The comparison matches top-level width, but the H-SAE has 16-64x more total atoms. The baseline uses an auxiliary dead-latent loss, the H-SAE uses orthogonality, l1 and top-level reconstruction terms; k=32 for both. No seeds or error bars.

statements.correction: Standard TopK SAE, Gemma 2-2B layer 20, 8k/16k/32k top-level latents. Absorption is plotted in Fig 5a (figure only). The text implies it grows with width.
statements.problem: The rise with width is implied by 'decreases the rate of increase', not stated directly. Layer 20 is the layer the training data comes from.

statements.correction: H-SAE (16 or 64 sublatents per expert) vs standard TopK SAE at matched top-level width (8k/16k/32k), Gemma 2-2B layer 20: lower absorption, slower rise with width; figure only.
statements.problem: Correct for this study. H-SAE lowers absorption (Fig 5a caption) and slows its growth with width (p.8), figure only. The limits_scope label fits: absorption persists, but its level depends on architecture. Minor point: 'fixed width' here means fixed top-level width. H-SAE has 16-64x more total atoms.

statements.correction: Standard SAE absorption rises from 8k to 32k per Fig 5a (figure only).
statements.problem: Only the text's implication and the figure support the rise.

statements.correction: Fig 5a: H-SAE has a lower mean absorption fraction than the standard TopK SAE at 8k-32k top-level latents; values figure only.
statements.problem: Correct. The text does not state the standard-vs-H-SAE comparison in numbers. H-SAE is mainly an architecture change, filed here under 'objectives'. V6.wording_issues[3] notes this.

statements.correction: The study does not check latents against the model's own units. Cross-language feature sharing in the LLM is cited, not tested.

statements.problem: The study measures absorption (SAEBench first-letter benchmark). The caption equates higher absorption with more splitting, but the study uses no separate splitting metric.

statements.correction: H-SAE changes the architecture (mixture-of-experts sublatent SAEs) and modifies the objective (eq. 3.2-3.4).
statements.problem: Correct. Strictly, the objective (3.2) adds three terms: top-level reconstruction (beta=0.1), bi-orthogonality and l1. Only the first is called important.

statements.correction: Fig 5b: English vs French mean top-8 symmetric set difference is 8.448 for H-SAE and 9.772 for the SAE; lower means more similar.
